title: Game 1: Marshall–Capablanca
subtitle: A delayed bishop and a missed tactical threat

source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Part II, Illustrative Games, Game 1: Queen’s Gambit Declined

narration.say: Marshall has White. Capablanca annotates his own loss and explains the shortcomings of his opening choices.
White exchanges bishops and develops the other bishop.
Black exchanges knights, but still has difficulty developing the bishop on c8.
White exchanges in the centre and brings the queen to b3. Black develops the knight.
White advances a4. Black challenges with c5, and the queen comes to a3.
Black plays b6. Capablanca criticises this move because it allows White to advance a5.
White castles. Black moves the queen to c7, and White brings the rook to b1.

steps.title: Find the bishop move Capablanca overlooked

narration.say: Capablanca says he did not see White’s threat. The bishop can attack the knight while gaining time against the queen.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Find the strong bishop move to f5.

feedback.*: Bishop from d3 to f5, attacking the knight on d7.

exercise.hint: Bishop from d3 to f5, attacking the knight on d7.

narration.say: White takes the knight. Black recaptures with the queen.
White advances a6. Black retreats the bishop, and the central exchange wins a pawn.
One pair of rooks is exchanged. White centralises the knight and supports it with f4.

steps.title: A queen sacrifice ends the game

narration.say: Black’s rook has reached b6. White can finish with a forcing queen sacrifice.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Capture the rook on b6.

narration.say: Capablanca resigned after queen takes b6. We stop where the book stops; no additional moves are played.
White combined the advanced a-pawn, active queen, and central knight. Black’s delayed development made the tactical threats harder to meet.
The author analyses his own mistakes rather than hiding them. That is a useful model for reviewing your games.
